1. Titanic Survival Analysis: EDA & Feature Engineering¶

1.1 Background¶

The RMS Titanic sank on April 15, 1912, after colliding with an iceberg in the North Atlantic. Of the 2,224 passengers and crew on board, only 710 survived.

This analysis investigates a question that the raw statistics alone cannot answer: Was survival random, or did socioeconomic status, gender, and family structure systematically determine who lived and who died?

1.2 Objective¶

  • Perform structured Exploratory Data Analysis on the Titanic passenger dataset.
  • Engineer meaningful features from raw columns to enrich the dataset.
  • Uncover the social and structural patterns that drove survival outcomes.
  • Prepare a clean, analysis-ready dataset for future machine learning modelling.

Note: No machine learning algorithms are applied in this notebook. The focus is entirely on understanding the data deeply before modelling begins and to perform EDA.

4. Data Dictionary and Variable Understanding¶

The training dataset contains 891 rows and 12 columns. Below is a reference guide to every variable.

4.1 Variable Reference Table¶

Column Type Description Notes
PassengerId Integer Unique ID assigned to each passenger Index only, no predictive value
Survived Integer (0/1) Target variable: 0 = Did not survive, 1 = Survived 38.4% survival rate
Pclass Integer (1/2/3) Ticket class: 1 = First, 2 = Second, 3 = Third Proxy for socioeconomic status
Name String Full passenger name including title Title (Mr, Mrs, Miss) can be extracted
Sex String Passenger gender: male / female Strong survival predictor
Age Float Age in years 19.9% values missing
SibSp Integer Number of siblings or spouses aboard Does not capture friends or colleagues
Parch Integer Number of parents or children aboard Combined with SibSp for family size
Ticket String Ticket number Contains prefix codes and shared tickets
Fare Float Total fare paid by the group, not per person Needs correction via feature engineering
Cabin String Cabin number 77.1% values missing; deck letter is extractable
Embarked String Port of embarkation: S = Southampton, C = Cherbourg, Q = Queenstown 2 values missing

4.2 Variable Classification¶

Numerical: Age, Fare, SibSp, Parch

Categorical (Nominal): Sex, Embarked, Cabin, Ticket

Categorical (Ordinal): Pclass

Target: Survived

To Drop: PassengerId, Name (after title extraction), Ticket (after prefix extraction)

5.2 Categorical cols¶

conclusions

  • Parch and SibSp cols can be merged to form a new col call family_size then giving us Family_type.
  • Embarked has 2 missing values and need to be filled, majority passengers embarked from Southampton.
  • Passenger class majority travelled in 3rd then 1st then 2nd, which is not natural.
  • Cabin can help in extracting the Deck position of passengers.
  • More than 60% passengers are male and rest are females.
  • Tickets are repetetive suggesting that there exists non family groups too.

6. Handling missing values¶

  • Age missing values can be replaced with mean age of passengers based on the class they are travelling.
  • Fare has only missing value no need for extra efforts and can be filled with mean fare.
  • Cabin and Deck has about 70% of missing vslues which can be assigned a dummy variable 'M'.
  • Embarked has 2 missing values, based on data Southamton has highest passenger embarking. So filling it with 'S'.
  • Calculation error in Individual fare column which can be filleed easily.
In [30]:
df_test = pd.read_csv('test.csv')
In [31]:
df_combine = pd.concat([df_train,df_test])
df_combine = df_combine.reset_index(drop=True)
In [32]:
df_combine.to_csv('concated.csv', index=False)

7. Feature Engineering¶

  • Fare was give the total amount paid by the family, need a new column with individual fare paid.
  • Sibling, spouse, parents, child are given seprately. They can be combined together to create family size and family type.
  • Titles can be extracted from names of passengers.
  • Deck can be extracted from Cabin number and missing values can be filled with a dummy variable 'M'.
  • Tickets are the gold mine in this dataset, we can extract Ticket prefix and frequency as many are repetetive implying that many passengers were travelling in friends/official/non-family groups which SibSp/ParCh failed to capture.

# family_type
# 1 -> alone
# 2-4 -> small
# >5 -> large

def transform_family_size(num):

  if num == 1:
    return 'alone'
  elif num>1 and num <5:
    return "small"
  else:
    return "large"

# Extracting Ticket prefix which indicates social classes among passengers
def extract_prefix(value):
    prefix=value.strip().split()
    if len(prefix)>1:
        prefix = prefix[0]                      # e.g. 'A/4', 'SOTON/O2', 'PC'
        prefix = prefix.split('/')[0]          # take only before the slash → 'A', 'SOTON', 'PC'
        prefix = prefix.split('.')[0]          # handle dots too e.g. 'A.4' → 'A'
        return prefix.upper()                  # normalize to uppercase
    else:
        return 'NUMERIC'

9. Bivariate Analysis¶
  • Survival chances are directly proportional to Higher class.
  • Survival chances of a females were significantly better than males.
  • Higher passengers survived who embarked from Cherbourg in comparison to other to station, because 50% people travelled in 1st class from Cherbourg where 46% of them being females.
  • Survival chances of small family were higher than passengers travelling alone or with large family.
  • Titles gives the same information as sex.

  • In Bivariate Analysis, we examined one variable against Survival at a time.
  • Multivariate Analysis lets us ask richer questions: "Did sex matter equally across all passenger classes?" or "Were children safer only if they were in 1st class?"
  • Here we combine 3+ variables to uncover interaction effects that simpler analysis misses.

df_clean['Pclass'] = df_clean['Pclass'].astype(str)
sns.stripplot(data=df_clean, y='Pclass', x='Sex',hue='Survived', palette=SURVIVAL_PALETTE, jitter= True)

df_clean['Pclass'] = df_clean['Pclass'].astype(int)

Insight — The Survival Privilege Gradient:

The Graph reveals a brutal inequality: 97.6% of 1st-class women survived, while only 50% of 3rd-class women did — despite the same "women first" protocol. For men, the class gradient is equally stark: a 1st-class man was 3× more likely to survive than a 3rd-class man. This tells us that both gender and class were independently driving survival — neither variable alone captures the full picture. A 3rd-class male passenger faced the most lethal combination of circumstances on the Titanic.

In [113]:
sns.catplot(data=df_clean, y='Age', x='Pclass', kind='violin', hue='Survived', palette=SURVIVAL_PALETTE, split=True, inner='quartile')
Out[113]:
<seaborn.axisgrid.FacetGrid at 0x20601560690>

Insight — Children Were Protected, But Only Partially:
In 1st and 2nd class, the violin shows that young children (left/green side) have strong survival — the bulge near age 0–10 is almost entirely on the survived side. In 3rd class, even children show a split survival distribution, suggesting that physical distance from lifeboats (3rd class cabins were at the bottom of the ship) created a lethal barrier that age alone couldn't overcome. The age signal is real, but class modifies how much it helps.

In [114]:
family_class = df_clean.groupby(['Pclass', 'family_type'])['Survived'].mean() * 100
family_class = family_class.reset_index()
sns.barplot(data=family_class ,x='family_type', y='Survived', hue='Pclass', palette='Set2', edgecolor='Black')

plt.show()

Insight — Family Safety Net Has a Class Ceiling:
Travelling in a small family (2–4 members) consistently improves survival odds across all classes — but the magnitude of the benefit depends on class. A small family in 1st class had ~70%+ survival, while a small family in 3rd class hovered near 30–40%. Large families (5+) suffered the most regardless of class — But in class 2 it shows 100% as there were only 2 families which survived (a statistical error) coordinating evacuation with many dependents likely cost precious time. Solo travellers in 3rd class faced the worst odds of any group.

11. Conclusions and Key Insights¶

will complete this after full analysis at last¶

  • Decided to keep the outliers(in Fare and Age). Since Fare and Age has deep correlation with survival

11.1 Executive Summary¶

The Titanic disaster of April 1912 is often described as a tragedy of fate. This analysis tells a different story, one of systematic inequality.

Survival on the Titanic was not random. It was shaped by a passenger's gender, the class they could afford, the family they travelled with, and the deck they slept on. The data, when examined carefully, reveals a social hierarchy that determined who lived and who died with uncomfortable precision.

11.2 Key Findings¶

Finding 1: Class Was a Matter of Life and Death¶

  • 1st class passengers had a ~63% survival rate vs only ~24% in 3rd class.
  • This gap cannot be explained by demographics alone, Sincce 3rd class cabins were located deep in the ship, far from the lifeboats, creating a physical barrier that money (or the lack of it) had quietly built long before the ship hit the iceberg.

Finding 2: "Women First" Was Real, But Class Modified It¶

  • ~97% of 1st class women survived. Only ~50% of 3rd class women did.
  • The "women and children first" protocol existed but it was enforced far more effectively on the upper decks. Gender protected you, but class decided how much.
  • 3rd class males faced the worst outcome of any group: under 15% survival rate.

Finding 3: Small Families Had a Survival Advantage¶

  • Passengers travelling in small families (2–4 members) consistently survived at higher rates than solo travellers or large families.
  • Large families (5+) in 3rd class faced the sharpest drop, coordinating evacuation with many dependents in a chaotic, unfamiliar lower deck likely cost critical minutes.
  • Caution: 100% survival for large families in 2nd class is misleading, the cell count is n < 5 and should not anchor any conclusion.

Finding 4: The Embarked Mystery (Solved)¶

  • Passengers from Cherbourg (C) appeared to survive more than Southampton (S) or Queenstown (Q) in bivariate analysis — seemingly puzzling.
  • Multivariate analysis resolved this: ~50% of Cherbourg passengers were 1st class, and a higher proportion were female. Cherbourg did not confer survival. It simply loaded a wealthier, higher-survival demographic. This is a textbook example of Simpson's Paradox in real data.

Finding 5: Tickets Reveal Hidden Social Groups¶

  • Ticket frequency exposed that many passengers shared a ticket without being family — travelling as friends, colleagues, or groups.
  • ~200 passengers were identified as part of a non-family group (same ticket, no family relation via SibSp/Parch) implies a signal that SibSp and Parch alone do not capture true travel group size.
  • Ticket prefixes correlated strongly with class: prefixes like PC, SC, F were almost exclusively 1st class, while CA, SOTON, W were 3rd class embedding social class in a seemingly arbitrary alphanumeric code.

Finding 6: Deck Position Echoed Class¶

  • Deck letters (A–F) followed the ship's physical layout: A was the top deck, F was near the bottom. Higher decks meant shorter paths to lifeboats.
  • Deck strongly tracked with Pclass: 1st class passengers occupied A, B, C while 3rd class filled F and G, making Deck a proxy for both class and physical escape distance.
  • 77% of Cabin/Deck values were missing, so conclusions here are directional rather than definitive.

Finding 7: Age Mattered, But Not Equally Across Classes¶

  • Children (age < 10) showed notably higher survival in 1st and 2nd class, the FacetGrid clearly showed a green bulge at low ages for these groups.
  • In 3rd class, even children showed a split survival distribution, suggesting that physical location on the ship eroded the "children first" advantage for the poorest passengers.

11.3 Feature Engineering: What We Built & Why It Mattered¶

Feature Built From Why It Matters
individual_fare Fare ÷ group size Group fare was misleading — this is the true ticket price per person
family_size SibSp + Parch + 1 Captures total travel companions
family_type family_size Categorises survival-relevant group sizes (alone / small / large)
Title Name Encodes gender + social status in one variable (Mr, Mrs, Miss, Master)
Deck Cabin Physical position on ship = proximity to lifeboats
Ticket_frequency Ticket True group size including non-family travel companions
Ticket_prefix Ticket Encodes social class and origin hidden inside ticket codes
non_family_group Ticket_frequency vs family_size Identifies passengers in friend/colleague groups missed by SibSp/Parch

The original dataset had 11 columns. After feature engineering, the enriched dataset has 19 meaningful columns, each grounded in domain reasoning not arbitrary transformation.

11.4 The Human Story Behind the Numbers¶

Strip away the statistics and what remains is this:

A 3rd class male passenger boarding at Southampton, travelling alone, had approximately a 1 in 8 chance of survival.
A 1st class female passenger boarding at Cherbourg, in a small family, had approximately a 9 in 10 chance of survival.

Same ship. Same night. Same iceberg. The difference was a ticket price.

The Titanic data does not just test machine learning models. It is a historical record of how wealth and gender shaped access to the most basic resource of all — a seat on a lifeboat.

11.5 Analyst's Honest Assessment: Limitations¶

  • Missing Cabin data (77%) limits Deck analysis. Conclusions on deck-level survival are directional at best.
  • Test set has no Survival labels — all survival-based analysis is on 891 training passengers, not the full 1309. Percentages may shift slightly on the full data.
  • Correlation ≠ Causation — individual_fare correlates with survival, but wealthier passengers didn't survive because they paid more. Wealth determined class, class determined deck, deck determined lifeboat access. The causal chain matters.
  • Small cell sizes in some group combinations (e.g., large family in 2nd class) make those percentages unreliable. Always check before concluding.

11.6 Next Steps: If This Were a Real Project¶

  • Machine Learning: The enriched feature set is now ready for a classification model (Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost). The engineered features especially Title, Deck, family_type, Ticket_prefix are expected to be among the top predictors.
  • Hyperparameter tuning on family_type boundaries (currently alone=1, small=2–4, large=5+) using survival rate curves to find the optimal cut-off.
  • Survival probability scoring: Assign each passenger a calculated survival probability based on weighted feature contributions a step toward explainable ML.
